newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - GKN tumbles on US court judgement fear.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - GKN tumbles on US court judgement fear.

text.p: British engineering giant GKN Plc saw its shares slide on Monday on fears that it could face demands for increased damages of $740 million in a lawsuit brought by its U.S. franchising operation.

Shares fell 26 pence to 969 pence per share by early afternoon, recovering from a 35 pence fall earlier following a report in the Financial Times which claimed lawyers acting for disgruntled U.S. franchises were increasing their maximum claim to $740 million.
GKN said on Monday it had heard nothing of the higher claim.
If granted, such a claim would be double the $398 million awarded to the plaintiffs, Meineke Discount Muffler Shops Inc, last December by a North Carolina jury.
GKN has not yet paid any damages as the case has still to be concluded.

However, this latest spectre of a higher claim means GKN faces the threat of having its entire 564 million pounds ($920.4 million) cash reserves erased coupled with a possible charge against profits, analysts said.
But a lot of the bad news is already factored in. "The worst of the news is already in the share price," said one analyst.
Meineke is a specialist exhaust retailer, wholly-owned by GKN, with a number of franchise agreements in the United States.

The U.S. franchisees, which trade under the name Meineke Discount Muffler Shops Inc, first filed a case against GKN in Charlotte in December 1993, citing allegations that included breach of contract related to advertising payments.
The claim arose from the administration of an advertising fund by GKN's unit Meineke. All franchisees contributed 10 percent of their weekly revenue to this fund.
The franchisees said the U.S. unit should only serve as "conduit or agent" of the advertising contributions.
But in 1986 Meineke set up an in-house advertising agency, New Horizons Advertising, which led to the plaintiffs claiming that this breached their agreement over the use of the funds.
GKN shares fell 35 1/2 pence to 1009 1/2 pence per share in the wake of last December's announcement on the case.
The new claim will be assessed by the presiding judge Robert Potter this Friday in the court at Charlotte.

The judge has a number of options: he can back the original award, raise it or cut it or order a retrial which will see the case starting from scratch again with a new jury, said GKN's director of public affairs Nicholas de Jongh.

But if GKN decides to appeal against the judge's decision, the next round will be assessed by three judges and no jury - a situation which analysts see benefiting GKN. One analyst said Friday's hearing was unlikely to be the end of the issue. "Whatever the award, the company is likely to appeal. So this will be a saga which will run and run," said Tony Lancelott of UBS.

Both sides have already made written responses to the judge following the jury's verdict last December. De Jongh said the "main thrust" of GKN's defence has been that it has acted within U.S. industry practice.
When the jury first announced the award against GKN last December, the British group predicted its maximum exposure was $554 million.

This worst case scenario reflected a ruling from the Charlotte district court stating that a part of the $398 million claim was made under the North Carolina Unfair Trade Practices Act, which carries a treble damages penalty. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
